material_systems.name: Clear / Transparent Wood Sealer

sealer.type: Penetrating clear water repellent with UV filter — no color pigment
products: Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced Clear Wood Protector
sealer.notes: Minimal UV protection — wood grain and natural color fully visible. Water repellent only. Best for new cedar fences where natural grain appearance is desired. Shortest maintenance cycle (1-2 years, annual recoat typical). Single coat application — re-apply at 12-18 month intervals. No primer required — sealer penetrates directly into wood fibers. Not recommended for PT pine (greenish chemical color shows through clear sealer).

material_systems.notes: Economy/minimal protection tier. No color matching. Fastest to apply. Lowest material cost per gallon but shortest maintenance cycle drives highest lifetime cost. Coverage varies by wood porosity: new smooth cedar ~300-350 SF/gal, new rough-sawn ~200-250 SF/gal, weathered restored ~200 SF/gal.

material_systems.name: Semi-Transparent Penetrating Stain

stain.type: Penetrating semi-transparent stain with iron oxide UV pigments
stain.notes: PROFESSIONAL STANDARD for residential wood fences (~55% of professional fence staining work). Iron oxide pigments provide UV protection while allowing wood grain visibility. Penetrating chemistry soaks into wood fibers — erodes gradually rather than peeling. 2-4 year maintenance cycle. Easy maintenance recoat (clean and recoat, no stripping). 1 coat on new wood with good absorption, 2 coats on weathered wood for color build. Most forgiving application — penetrating stain hides minor application inconsistencies. No primer required. Hides PT pine green tint while showing wood texture.

material_systems.notes: Standard residential fence recommendation. Best balance of protection, aesthetics, and maintainability. Coverage is porosity-dependent: new smooth wood at higher end of range, weathered/porous wood at lower end. Back-brushing mandatory when spray-applied to force stain into wood grain. Oil-based formulations preferred on cedar for better tannin resistance.

material_systems.name: Solid Color Fence Stain

stain.type: Film-forming solid body stain — opaque color, complete grain masking
products: Cabot Solid Color Acrylic Deck & Siding Stain
stain.notes: Maximum UV protection — film-forming coating that completely masks wood grain. Opaque color. 3-7 year cycle on vertical fence surfaces (longer than decks because no foot traffic wear). Good for hiding wood defects, knots, color inconsistency, or previous stain color. Requires more prep for maintenance recoat (sand, possibly strip if failing). Two coats mandatory with full dry between coats. Tannin-blocking primer REQUIRED on cedar substrates (SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK).

material_systems.notes: Good option for color matching to house or covering weathered/mismatched wood. Vertical fence surfaces have lower delamination risk than horizontal deck surfaces (better water shedding, no foot traffic). Tannin-blocking primer mandatory on cedar. Coverage is higher than penetrating stains because film sits on surface rather than absorbing. ~30% of professional fence staining work.

material_systems.name: Exterior Latex Paint (LEAST RECOMMENDED for wood fences)

paint.type: 100% acrylic exterior latex paint — HIGH permeability formulation critical
products: Benjamin Moore Regal Select Exterior Paint
paint.dft_mils: 4-6 mils total (2 coats at 2-3 mils each)
paint.notes: WARNING — LEAST RECOMMENDED coating type for wood fences. Paint forms a film that traps moisture migrating through fence from both sides. Fences are fully exposed to weather on BOTH faces — unlike walls where one side is protected. Moisture trapped under paint film causes blistering, peeling, and premature failure — often within 2-3 years on the weather side. If paint is specified: use HIGH PERMEABILITY (breathable) formulation to allow maximum moisture vapor transmission. 100% acrylic mandatory for flexibility. Two coats required. Full primer required (SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK on cedar, standard exterior primer on PT pine). 5-10 year theoretical cycle but expect earlier failure on weather-exposed face.

material_systems.notes: ~10% of fence work. Used when HOA mandates white fences, customer insists on specific paint color, or color matching to house paint. MANDATORY risk warning when specified — document moisture-peeling risk in project record with customer acknowledgment. Highest failure rate of all fence coating options.

material_systems.name: Alkyd Stain-Blocking Primer (cedar / tannin management)

primer.type: Alkyd stain-blocking exterior primer — prevents tannin bleed through film-forming topcoats
primer.notes: MANDATORY on cedar substrates before solid stain or paint application. Cedar contains water-soluble extractive tannins that bleed through water-based film-forming coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration. Alkyd/oil-based primer formula seals tannins in wood. Shellac-based alternatives (BIN) provide superior tannin blocking but have higher VOC and cost. Apply to both faces of fence. Also used as standard exterior primer for paint option on PT pine substrates.

material_systems.notes: Conditional system — only activated when substrate_material = cedar AND coating_type = solid_stain or paint. NOT used with penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent) — primer seals wood and prevents stain penetration. Also serves as the standard exterior primer for the paint coating_type on PT pine (paint always requires primer regardless of substrate).

material_systems.name: Fence Cleaner / Stripper (Alkaline)

prep_chemical.type: Alkaline wood cleaner/stripper — sodium hydroxide or sodium percarbonate based, pH 12-14
products: Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck Revive Deck & Fence Cleaner
prep_chemical.notes: First step in chemical restoration protocol for weathered or previously coated wood fences. Removes failed coating residue, mildew, dirt, UV-degraded fiber, and opens wood pores. Apply with pump sprayer or brush, allow to dwell 10-15 minutes, scrub with stiff bristle brush, rinse with garden hose or low-pressure washer. MUST be neutralized with acid brightener (SYS_EXT_FNCE_BRIGHTENER) before staining — alkaline residue prevents proper stain adhesion and penetration. Chemical runoff onto landscaping below fence requires protection.

material_systems.notes: Not used on new bare wood (SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD) — new wood prep is seasoning verification and optional mill glaze removal, not chemical stripping. Coverage varies by contamination level: heavily soiled/failed coatings consume more product. Vertical fence surfaces drain well — faster rinse cycle than horizontal decks.

material_systems.name: Wood Brightener (Oxalic / Citric Acid)

prep_chemical.type: Oxalic acid or citric acid wood brightener, pH 1.5-2.5
prep_chemical.notes: Second step in chemical restoration protocol. Neutralizes alkaline stripper residue, restores natural wood color by dissolving surface tannin deposits, and lowers wood surface pH to 3.5-4.5 (optimal for stain adhesion). Oxalic acid formula preferred for cedar tannin management. Citric acid as milder alternative. MANDATORY after alkaline stripping — never stain over alkaline residue. Also used standalone on cedar substrates (even new wood) to manage tannin bleed before staining. Apply with pump sprayer or brush, allow 10-15 minutes, rinse thoroughly. Allow 12-24 hours drying before staining (shorter than deck's 24-48 hours due to vertical drainage).

material_systems.notes: On cedar, brightener is used even on new bare wood (SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD) for tannin management — this is the substrate_material_override scenario. On PT pine, brightener is only used after alkaline stripping (weathered/previously_coated conditions). Vertical fences dry faster than horizontal decks — 12-24 hours vs 24-48 hours.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth (planed) fence boards. Lower absorption — sealer sits closer to surface. Less common on fences than decks — most fence boards are rough-sawn.

new_rough_sawn.notes: New rough-sawn fence boards. Open fiber structure absorbs more product. Most common surface condition for new fences (cedar and PT pine).

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered wood after chemical restoration. Open pores from UV damage absorb more product despite restoration. Vertical surface drains better than deck — slightly less pooling loss.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain at top of fence boards and post tops absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain. Factor 0.40 means 40% of normal coverage = 2.5x material consumption. Significant on fences due to exposed board tops along entire fence length.

assumptions: Coverage per single coat application with brush, pump sprayer, or spray_backbrush.
Spray_backbrush adds ~15-20% material for overspray (varies by fence_style).
End-grain areas (board tops, post tops) consume 2-3x normal — captured in end_grain_modifier.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth fence boards. Moderate absorption. Single coat typically sufficient on new wood.

new_rough_sawn.notes: New rough-sawn fence boards. Higher absorption into open fiber structure. Most common fence surface condition.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered wood after chemical restoration. Most porous condition — highest material consumption. Two coats typical for color build on weathered substrate.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more stain. Factor 0.40 = ~2.5x material consumption on end-grain areas (board tops, post tops).

assumptions: Coverage per coat. New wood typically 1 coat, weathered wood typically 2 coats.
Spray_backbrush adds ~15-20% material for overspray (fence_style dependent).
Oil-based and water-based semi-transparent stains have comparable coverage rates — open time differs but absorption is similar.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth fence boards. Film-forming product builds on surface — minimal absorption. Highest coverage of fence stain types.

new_rough_sawn.notes: Rough-sawn texture increases surface area and absorbs some product before film forms.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered restored wood. Porous substrate absorbs first coat more heavily. Second coat achieves better coverage.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorption is less severe with solid stain (film-forming). Factor 0.60 = ~1.7x material consumption on end-grain.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. Two coats mandatory with full dry between coats.
Spray adds ~20% material for overspray (film-forming generates more mist than penetrating).
Solid stain coverage is comparable to exterior paint — film sits on surface rather than absorbing.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth fence boards over primer. Film-forming — highest coverage rate. Similar to solid stain.

new_rough_sawn.notes: Rough-sawn absorbs more paint despite primer undercoat. Primer reduces but does not eliminate porosity-driven absorption.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered restored wood over primer. Primer coat normalizes surface but residual porosity remains.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorption mitigated by primer coat. Factor 0.60 = ~1.7x material consumption on end-grain.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. Two coats mandatory.
Primer coat applied first (SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK) — primer coverage is separate profile.
Spray adds ~20% material for overspray.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth fence boards. Primer sits on surface — high coverage rate.

new_rough_sawn.notes: Rough-sawn absorbs primer into open fiber. Standard fence surface.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered restored wood. Porous substrate absorbs more primer.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorbs primer heavily. Factor 0.50 = ~2x material consumption. Sealing end-grain is critical for tannin blocking at board tops.

assumptions: Coverage per single coat.
Alkyd primer on cedar for tannin blocking. Also serves as standard primer for paint option on PT pine.
Spray adds ~15-20% material for overspray.

standard.notes: Coverage varies by contamination level. Heavily soiled or multi-layer failed coatings may require double application at lower end of range.

assumptions: Single application. May require second application on heavily contaminated surfaces.
Apply with pump sprayer or brush. Pump sprayer more efficient for large fence runs.
Dwell time 10-15 minutes before scrubbing and rinsing.
Vertical fence surface drains well — less product pooling than horizontal deck.

standard.notes: Consistent coverage regardless of wood condition — acid brightener is applied evenly. Cedar may require slightly more product for tannin dissolution.

assumptions: Single application. Cedar tannin management may require extended dwell time but not necessarily more product.
Apply with pump sprayer or brush. Allow 10-15 minutes, rinse thoroughly.
12-24 hours drying after brightener application before staining (shorter than deck's 24-48 hours due to vertical drainage).

consumables.name: Stiff synthetic bristle brush 4-6 inch (back-brush / stain application)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 500 SF of fence back-brushing or 80 LF of post/detail brushwork
consumables.notes: MANDATORY for spray_backbrush application — forces penetrating stain into wood grain pores. Also used as primary brush for split rail, post detail, and gate staining. Stiff synthetic bristle (not soft-tip) for maximum stain working into grain. 4-6 inch width for panel faces, 2-3 inch for posts and gate detail. Stain degrades bristles faster than paint — replace more frequently. Two-person crew: one sprays, one back-brushes.

consumables.name: Detail brush 2-3 inch (posts, gates, pickets, end-grain)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 40 LF of post/rail detail or 50 EA pickets
consumables.notes: Smaller brush for detail staining: fence posts, post caps, gate frames, picket tops, end-grain treatment. Stiff synthetic bristle. Replace when bristles soften or fray. End-grain at board tops requires dedicated pass with extra product.

consumables.name: Airless spray tip 517 (wide fan for fence panels)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 2,000-3,000 SF of spray coverage
consumables.notes: 517 tip = 10 inch fan width, 0.017 inch orifice. Wide fan pattern for fence panel faces — covers standard 6 ft fence height in 1-2 passes. Used with airless sprayer for solid stain and paint. For penetrating stains, pump sprayer or HVLP preferred over airless. Replace when fan pattern becomes uneven or tails appear.

consumables.name: Airless spray tip 413 (narrow fan for posts and detail)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 1,500-2,500 SF equivalent of detail spray coverage
consumables.notes: 413 tip = 8 inch fan width, 0.013 inch orifice. Narrower fan for fence posts, gate frames, and picket detail work. Lower flow rate reduces overspray on narrow components. Used with solid stain and paint options.

consumables.name: Pump sprayer (2-gallon, for stain and prep chemical application)
consumables.notes: Hand-pump sprayer for applying penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent) and chemical prep products (stripper, brightener). NOT an airless sprayer — penetrating stains use pump sprayer or HVLP, not high-pressure airless (which atomizes too finely for penetrating products). Clean between products — do NOT cross-contaminate alkaline stripper and acid brightener. Dedicated sprayers recommended for alkaline and acid products.

consumables.name: Pressure washer (1,200-1,500 PSI for fence cleaning)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per project (daily rental or owned)
consumables.notes: For fence cleaning and rinsing chemical products. Fan tip (25-40 degree) at 1,200-1,500 PSI maximum for fences (lower than deck due to thinner fence boards). WARNING: higher pressure damages wood fibers, blows out board joints, and can split thin fence pickets. Keep nozzle 10-14 inches from surface. Sweep WITH the grain. Used for cleaning existing fences and rinsing chemical restoration products.

consumables.name: Stiff bristle scrub brush (chemical prep)
consumables.notes: Heavy-duty stiff bristle brush for working chemical stripper and brightener into wood surface during dwell time. Poly or tampico bristle — not wire (wire embeds in wood and rust-stains). Long-handle push broom style for vertical fence panels.

consumables.name: Sanding disc 80-100 grit (weathered fiber removal / light prep)
consumables.notes: For removing loose fibers on weathered wood after chemical restoration, or light sanding to improve adhesion on previously coated surfaces. Random orbital sander. 80 grit for fiber removal, 100 grit for surface smoothing. Less sanding needed on fences than decks (no foot traffic wear pattern to address).

consumables.name: Pin-type electronic moisture meter (verification tool)
consumables.notes: MANDATORY verification tool. Electronic pin-type moisture meter for wood MC reading. MC must be < 19% for PT pine, < 15% for cedar before any stain application (HARD STOP if above). Take readings at 6-8 locations along fence (both sides, shaded areas, areas near ground/sprinklers). Water bead test is supplemental field check only — moisture meter is authoritative.

consumables.name: Painter's tape (exterior grade, UV-resistant)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 ROLL (60 yd) per 30 LF of masking lines
consumables.notes: UV-resistant exterior masking tape for protecting house siding at fence-to-house tie point, gate hardware masking, and any smooth-surface fixtures near fence. 14-day removal rating minimum. Standard blue painter's tape. Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Plastic sheeting (4 mil, UV-resistant)
consumables.notes: For siding protection at fence-to-house junction during spray operations. Landscape/hardscape protection along fence base on both sides. Vehicle protection when parked near fence spray zone. 4 mil minimum for durability. UV-resistant for multi-day projects.

consumables.name: Canvas drop cloths
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 100 SF hardscape coverage or 50 LF fence base runner
consumables.notes: For protecting adjacent hardscape (walkways, driveways, patios) along fence base from stain drip and overspray. Non-slip surface for crew traffic. Laid as runners along fence line on both sides. Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Stir sticks and mixing containers
consumables.usage_rate: 2 EA stir sticks per gallon + 1 mixing bucket per 5 gallons
consumables.notes: Penetrating stains require thorough stirring before and during application — pigments settle faster than in latex paint. Box multiple gallons in a 5-gallon bucket for color consistency across the entire fence. CRITICAL: color consistency is especially important on fences because both sides of every section are visible.

consumables.name: Gate hardware masking supplies (tape, plastic bags)
consumables.notes: Masking materials for gate hardware: hinges (2-3 per gate), latch mechanism, lock cylinder, decorative hardware. Blue tape + small plastic bags. Remove gate handle/latch if accessible for cleaner stain line. 10-15 minutes masking time per gate.

ext_landscape_fence_base.description: Landscaping, mulch beds, and ground cover along fence base on both sides
ext_landscape_fence_base.notes: Drop cloth/plastic runners along fence base on BOTH sides. Primary overspray and drip protection zone. LF along fence line x 2 sides. Brush application: light drip protection (canvas runners). Spray_backbrush: full cover with plastic (tape at fence base, extend 3-4 ft out from fence).

ext_hardscape_fence_adjacent.description: Walkways, driveways, patios running along fence line
ext_hardscape_fence_adjacent.notes: Canvas drop cloth runners for non-slip crew traffic areas. Plastic sheeting for overspray protection on areas without foot traffic. Stain overspray on concrete is extremely difficult to remove — penetrating product absorbs into concrete pores.

ext_siding_at_fence_tie.description: House siding where fence attaches to structure
ext_siding_at_fence_tie.condition: when fence ties into house siding
ext_siding_at_fence_tie.notes: Tape and plastic at fence-to-house junction. Fence typically ties into house at garage or side yard. Brush application: tape at junction only. Spray: plastic drape on siding face from fence level up 4-6 ft, taped at top edge.

ext_vehicle_adjacent.description: Vehicles parked near fence being sprayed (driveway fences)
ext_vehicle_adjacent.notes: Vehicles parked near fence being sprayed. Overspray drift onto vehicles is a liability risk. Full cover with plastic sheeting or relocate vehicles. Always spray away from vehicles when possible. Per vehicle.

ext_neighbor_property.description: Neighbor's landscaping, structures, and items near fence on opposite side
ext_neighbor_property.condition: when spraying fence side facing neighbor
ext_neighbor_property.notes: Neighbor's landscaping, structures, and items near fence. Drop cloth along neighbor's side of fence base. Coordinate with neighbor before work begins. Wind drift is primary concern — spray away from neighbor's property when possible.

compatibility_rules.description: Moisture content must be below threshold before any coating application
compatibility_rules.required_action: Moisture test with pin-type electronic moisture meter. PT pine: MC > 19% = HARD STOP. Cedar: MC > 15% = HARD STOP. Reschedule.
compatibility_rules.notes: MC above threshold prevents stain penetration (penetrating stains) and causes adhesion failure (solid stain/paint). Electronic pin-type moisture meter is the authoritative measurement. Water bead test is supplemental field check only. PT pine has higher MC tolerance (19%) than cedar (15%) on vertical fence surfaces.

compatibility_rules.description: New pressure-treated pine requires 3-6 month seasoning before staining
compatibility_rules.required_action: HARD STOP if wood age < 3 months. Verify seasoning with builder/GC. 6 months preferred.
compatibility_rules.notes: New PT lumber contains waterborne preservatives (ACQ, CA-B, MCA) that leave wood saturated with copper compounds and moisture. Staining green PT wood results in poor penetration, blotchy appearance, and premature coating failure. This is the most common fence staining callback. Project-level gate — verify BEFORE scheduling.

compatibility_rules.description: Paint on wood fences — MANDATORY moisture-peeling risk warning
compatibility_rules.required_action: Document moisture-driven peeling risk in project record with customer acknowledgment. Recommend semi-transparent or solid stain as alternative. Proceed only with documented customer acceptance.
compatibility_rules.notes: Paint on wood fences = highest failure rate of all coating options. Moisture migrates through fence from both sides (fully exposed to weather). Film traps moisture causing blistering and peeling, often within 2-3 years. This is NOT a hard stop — paint is a valid customer choice (HOA, color matching) — but risk MUST be documented.

compatibility_rules.description: Cedar requires tannin-blocking primer before solid stain or paint
compatibility_rules.notes: Cedar contains water-soluble extractive tannins that bleed through water-based film-forming coatings causing dark brown/red discoloration. Alkyd stain-blocking primer seals tannins. MANDATORY on cedar with solid stain or paint. Shellac-based alternatives provide superior blocking. Oil-based stain products (semi-transparent) resist tannin bleed better than water-based on cedar.

compatibility_rules.description: Cedar requires oxalic acid brightener for tannin management
compatibility_rules.notes: Oxalic acid brightener dissolves surface tannins before staining. MANDATORY on cedar regardless of wood condition (new or weathered). On new cedar, brightener manages surface tannins. On weathered cedar, brightener is part of full chemical restoration protocol.

compatibility_rules.description: Never apply stain over degraded gray wood without restoration
compatibility_rules.required_action: Chemical restoration (SYS_EXT_FNCE_CHEMICAL_STRIPPER + SYS_EXT_FNCE_BRIGHTENER) OR mechanical sanding required before staining.
compatibility_rules.notes: UV-degraded gray wood has loose cellulose fibers and degraded lignin on the surface. Stain applied over gray wood bonds to loose fibers, not sound wood — coating fails prematurely as loose fibers detach. Chemical restoration or sanding removes degraded surface layer to expose sound wood.

compatibility_rules.description: Alkaline stripper must be neutralized with acid brightener before staining
compatibility_rules.notes: Alkaline wood cleaner/stripper (pH 12-14) leaves alkaline residue on wood surface that prevents proper stain adhesion and penetration. Acid brightener (pH 1.5-2.5) neutralizes residue and restores wood pH to 3.5-4.5 (optimal for stain adhesion). NEVER skip brightener step after alkaline stripping.

compatibility_rules.description: Penetrating stains do NOT use primer — primer blocks stain penetration
compatibility_rules.notes: Primer seals the wood surface and PREVENTS stain penetration — the opposite of the desired effect. Penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent) must be applied directly to bare or prepared wood. The prime-then-paint pipeline does not apply to penetrating stains.

compatibility_rules.description: Back-brushing mandatory when spray-applying penetrating stains
compatibility_rules.required_action: Spray deposits stain on surface only — back-brush immediately with stiff synthetic bristle brush to force stain into wood grain. No spray-only option for penetrating stains.
compatibility_rules.notes: Same mandate as deck spec. Spray-only application of penetrating stains is NOT acceptable. Two-person crew: one sprays, one follows immediately with back-brush. Back-brushing also helps work stain into board-to-board joints and end-grain at board tops.

compatibility_rules.description: Paint option on PT pine requires exterior primer
compatibility_rules.notes: Paint on any wood fence substrate requires primer coat for adhesion. PT pine does not need tannin blocking but still requires exterior primer before paint topcoat. SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK serves dual duty as tannin blocker on cedar and standard primer on PT pine.

spray_waste_factors.description: Spray application material waste factors by fence style — accounts for overspray, wind drift, and spray-through losses

privacy.notes: Solid panel catches most spray. Lowest waste. Overspray at fence top and ends only.

shadowbox.notes: Alternating boards on both sides create gaps. Angle spray required to reach recessed faces. Moderate overspray through gaps.

picket.notes: Highest waste — gaps between pickets allow spray-through. Individual pickets with small target area. Most overspray of any fence style.

split_rail.notes: Split rail fences are brush-applied. No spray waste factor applies.

spray_waste_factors.notes: Waste factors are applied to material quantity calculations, NOT to labor rates. Material ordering must include waste factor. Wind conditions increase waste above these baselines.

risk_notes.topic: Moisture-driven peeling on painted wood fences
risk_notes.risk: Paint forms a film on both fence faces that traps moisture migrating through wood from rain exposure on either side. Unlike a wall (one side protected), a fence is exposed on BOTH sides. Moisture enters from the weather side, migrates through wood, becomes trapped under paint on the lee side. Causes blistering, bubbling, and sheet peeling — often within 2-3 years. The weather-exposed face fails first.
risk_notes.mitigation: Use penetrating stains instead of paint on wood fences. If paint is specified, document risk warning with customer acknowledgment. Use premium 100% acrylic with high permeability rating. Ensure wood MC below threshold. Back-prime all boards (both faces).

risk_notes.topic: Premature stain failure on unseasoned PT pine
risk_notes.risk: Stain applied to new PT pine that has not seasoned (< 3 months since treatment) fails to penetrate properly. Waterborne preservatives and excess moisture repel stain. Result: blotchy, uneven appearance within weeks, complete stain failure within first season. Most common fence staining callback.
risk_notes.mitigation: HARD STOP: verify PT pine seasoning age >= 3 months (6 months preferred). Perform water bead test. Verify MC < 19%. If wood is too new, schedule staining for later date. Do not apply stain to green PT wood under any circumstances.

risk_notes.topic: Cedar tannin bleed-through on film-forming coatings
risk_notes.risk: Water-soluble extractive tannins in cedar bleed through solid stain and paint coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration streaks. Most severe with water-based coatings and at end-grain locations (top of fence boards). Tannin bleed stains adjacent surfaces (concrete walkways, driveways) when washed by rain.
risk_notes.mitigation: For penetrating stains: accept some tannin bleed as natural. For solid stain/paint: use tannin-blocking primer (SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK). Consider oil-based stain for better tannin resistance. Treat with oxalic acid brightener before coating to dissolve surface tannins.

risk_notes.risk: Applying too much penetrating stain creates a thick surface film on what should be an absorbed-into-wood finish. Common when back-brushing is skipped (spray pooling in board joints and bottom edges) or when recoating over still-wet first coat. Excess forms a sticky, tacky film that does not cure properly, attracts dirt, and peels.
risk_notes.mitigation: Apply thin coats. Back-brush thoroughly to work stain into wood and remove excess from surface. Do not allow pooling at board joints, bottom edges, or horizontal rails. Allow first coat to absorb before second coat. Wipe excess from non-absorbing surfaces (fastener heads, hardware).

risk_notes.topic: Wind drift overspray on adjacent property and vehicles
risk_notes.risk: Fences are fully exposed outdoor structures with no containment. Wind carries spray mist onto neighbor's property, vehicles, landscaping, and structures. Stain overspray on vehicles and concrete is difficult to remove. Liability risk is highest with spray application on windy days.
risk_notes.mitigation: Do not spray when wind exceeds 10 mph. Spray away from neighbor's property and vehicles. Full cover protection on vehicles within 20 ft of fence. Coordinate with neighbor before work. Canvas/plastic runners along both sides of fence base. Consider brush application if wind conditions are marginal.

risk_notes.risk: Alkaline stripper (pH 12-14) and acid brightener (pH 1.5-2.5) are chemically incompatible. Cross-contamination in pump sprayers, brushes, or mixing containers causes neutralization reaction that renders both products ineffective.
risk_notes.mitigation: Use dedicated pump sprayers for alkaline and acid products — label clearly. Rinse all application tools thoroughly between products. Allow alkaline stripper to be fully rinsed from surface before applying acid brightener.

risk_notes.topic: Pressure washer damage to thin fence boards
risk_notes.risk: Fence boards are thinner than deck boards (typically 5/8 to 3/4 inch vs 1-1.5 inch for decking). Pressure washing at too high PSI damages wood fibers, blows out board joints, and can split thin fence pickets. Damage creates fuzzy raised grain and uneven stain absorption.
risk_notes.mitigation: Maximum 1,200-1,500 PSI with fan tip (25-40 degree) for fence cleaning (lower than deck's 1,500-2,000 PSI). Keep nozzle 10-14 inches from surface. Sweep WITH the grain. Never use zero-degree (turbo) nozzle on fence boards. If fibers are raised, light sanding (80-100 grit) required before staining.

material_quantity_notes.spray_transfer_efficiency: Pump sprayer for penetrating stains: ~80-85% transfer efficiency (low-pressure, minimal overspray). Airless sprayer for solid stain/paint: ~65-75% transfer efficiency. Back-brushing redistributes overspray — actual waste is lower than wall spraying because excess is worked into wood.
material_quantity_notes.wood_porosity_factor: New smooth: 1.00x. New rough-sawn: 1.25-1.40x. Weathered/restored: 1.30-1.50x. Applied on top of base coverage rate. Most fence boards are rough-sawn — rough-sawn is the default assumption for fences.
material_quantity_notes.end_grain_factor: End-grain (top of fence boards, post tops, rail ends) absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain. Fences have significant end-grain exposure along the entire top edge. Budget additional material for end-grain treatment pass.
material_quantity_notes.both_sides_note: PaintScope delivers FINAL SF that includes both sides of the fence (LF x Height x 2 x style_multiplier). Material calculation uses this total SF. Do NOT double the PaintScope SF.
material_quantity_notes.coat_count_by_system: Transparent: 1 coat. Semi-transparent: 1 coat (new wood), 2 coats (weathered). Solid stain: 2 coats mandatory. Paint: 2 coats mandatory. Primer (when applicable): 1 coat. Chemical stripper: 1 application. Brightener: 1 application.
material_quantity_notes.fence_style_waste_factors: Privacy: 15-20% spray waste. Shadowbox: 20-25%. Picket: 25-30%. Split rail: n/a (brush only). Include in material quantity calculation, NOT in labor rate.
material_quantity_notes.boxing_requirement: CRITICAL: Box (mix) all gallons of stain into a single container before application to ensure color consistency. Both sides of every fence section are visible — color inconsistency between cans is immediately apparent.

assumptions.value: 200-350 SF/gal for penetrating stains, varying by coating type, wood condition, and wood species
assumptions.source: Exterior_Fences_Doctrine.md; research.json RF-001, RF-008; deck sibling materials.json
assumptions.note: Coverage profiles refined by wood condition (new smooth vs rough-sawn vs weathered). Conservative midpoints used for estimation. Fence coverage rates are similar to deck rates — same wood substrates and stain chemistry.

assumptions.value: 250-400 SF/gal — higher than penetrating stains due to film-forming chemistry
assumptions.note: Film-forming products (solid stain, paint) build on surface rather than absorbing. Coverage comparable to exterior paint on smooth surfaces.

assumptions.value: 150-250 SF/gal for alkaline stripper and acid brightener
assumptions.source: research.json RF-011; deck sibling materials.json; manufacturer PDS data
assumptions.note: Doctrine does not specify exact coverage rates for fence chemical prep products. Derived from manufacturer data and deck sibling patterns. Flag for field calibration.

assumptions.value: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain
assumptions.source: research.json RF-012; deck sibling materials.json; wood science principles
assumptions.note: Doctrine mentions end-grain absorption risk but does not quantify the multiplier. 2-3x is wood science standard. Fence end-grain exposure is significant — entire top edge of fence boards is end-grain.

assumptions.value: Rough-sawn is the default/most common fence board surface (unlike decks where smooth is common)
assumptions.note: Most fence boards are rough-sawn or dog-eared rough. Smooth/planed fence boards are less common. Default coverage estimates should use rough-sawn rates.

assumptions.value: 1,200-1,500 PSI maximum for fences (vs 1,500-2,000 PSI for decks)
assumptions.source: research.json notes_for_materials_manager; thin board damage risk
assumptions.note: Fence boards are thinner than deck boards. Lower PSI required to prevent fiber damage, joint blowout, and board splitting. Not explicitly in doctrine — derived from material thickness difference.

uncertainty_flags.topic: End-grain material consumption along fence top edge
uncertainty_flags.description: Fences have continuous end-grain exposure along the entire top edge (every board top). The end-grain modifier (2-3x) applies to a larger proportional area than on decks. On a 100 LF fence, the top edge represents significant end-grain area. Material consumption for the end-grain treatment pass may be underestimated.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Material ordering may be short by 10-15% if end-grain consumption along fence top is underestimated.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Field measurement data from fence staining projects comparing actual stain consumption with end-grain treatment vs theoretical coverage.

uncertainty_flags.description: Shadowbox fences have a corrugated profile with alternating boards on both sides. The 20-25% spray waste factor is an estimate. Actual waste depends on board width, gap width, overlap depth, and spray angle achievable. Tight shadowbox (narrow gaps) may have lower waste; wide-gap shadowbox higher.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Material ordering for shadowbox fences may be off by 10-15% in either direction.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Field calibration data from shadowbox fence spray projects with measured material consumption vs theoretical coverage.

uncertainty_flags.topic: Oil-based vs water-based stain coverage difference on cedar
uncertainty_flags.description: Coverage profiles do not differentiate between oil-based and water-based stains. Oil-based stains may have deeper penetration on cedar (better tannin resistance) but different coverage characteristics. Research recommends oil-based for cedar but coverage data is not split by chemistry.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Low — coverage ranges are wide enough to accommodate both chemistries.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: If doctrine establishes oil-based vs water-based stain distinction for cedar, split coverage profiles accordingly.

uncertainty_flags.description: SYS_EXT_FNCE_PRIMER_STAIN_BLOCK serves dual duty: tannin-blocking primer on cedar (alkyd formula critical) and standard exterior primer on PT pine for paint option. Coverage rates may differ slightly between cedar and PT pine substrates due to different wood porosity and tannin absorption.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Low — coverage ranges are broad enough to accommodate both substrates.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Consider splitting into two primer systems if field data shows > 15% coverage difference between cedar and PT pine.
